**The Alchemy of Forgotten Things**

I found the book in the attic last summer—half-buried under yellowed newspapers and a rusted teapot that smelled of rain and old love letters. The title was faded: *The Last Library of Eldermere*. The pages were brittle, the ink smudged as if someone had tried to erase something. I didn’t know what to do with it at first. Libraries are places of order, of cataloged knowledge, but this was a relic, a whisper from a time when books were not just stored but *lived in*. The spine curled like a sleeping creature, and when I turned it open, the first line jumped off the page:

*"They say the library was built from the bones of a thousand forgotten poets."*

I should have thrown it away. But then I remembered the way my grandmother used to read aloud to me from books that had been passed down through generations—books that weren’t just stories, but *echoes of voices*. That night, I sat in the dim light of my bedroom, fingers trembling as I turned the pages. The words didn’t make sense at first. The language was old, the grammar twisted like vine roots. But then, slowly, the story unfolded.

It was about a city called Eldermere, where the air hummed with the ghosts of those who had written before them. The library wasn’t just a place—it was a *breathing thing*, a living archive where words were not just read but *consumed*, like food. The poets who lived there didn’t just write; they *became* their words, their thoughts bleeding into the ink, into the paper. And when the last poet died, the library began to fade. The books turned to dust. The walls wept ink. The city forgot its own name.

But the book I held wasn’t just a story. It was a *warning*. Because now, the library was gone. And the poets were gone. And the words that had once filled the pages were slipping away, swallowed by the silence of the world.

I didn’t know what to do. Should I burn it? Bury it? Or—*gasp*—keep it? The attic was already too full of things that had been forgotten, that had been *erased* by time. But then I thought of the way my grandfather used to say, *"Some things are worth saving, even if they’re broken."* So I tucked the book under my pillow that night. And when I woke up, I found it there, untouched.

The next morning, I went back to the attic. The rusted teapot was gone. The newspapers were still there, but the corners were crisp, as if someone had just folded them. And in the place where the book had been, there was now a single, perfect page—white, blank, waiting.

I don’t know what happened. Maybe the book was a spell. Maybe it was a promise. But now, every night, when I close my eyes, I hear a faint whisper in the dark—a voice, just for a second, saying:

*"Write again."*

And I do.
